exam2.question: A 6-week-old with progressive ventriculomegaly after intraventricular hemorrhage has an anterior cerebral artery RI of 0.80 at rest that rises markedly when gentle pressure is applied to the anterior fontanelle. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: Normal response expected in all infants
Cerebral hyperperfusion from loss of autoregulation
Impaired intracranial compliance suggesting raised intracranial pressure
Venous sinus thrombosis with collateral flow

exam2.explanation: A marked RI increase with fontanelle compression indicates poor intracranial compliance and supports raised pressure that may need CSF diversion. Hyperperfusion would lower, not raise, the RI.
exam2.hint: Consider what added external pressure does to diastolic flow when the intracranial space has little reserve.

exam2.question: A newborn has a large posterior fossa cyst that communicates directly with a dilated fourth ventricle. The cerebellar vermis is small and rotated upward, the torcula is elevated, and there is lateral ventricular dilation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle with vermian hypoplasia and an enlarged posterior fossa with elevated torcula defines Dandy-Walker malformation. Mega cisterna magna has an intact vermis and normal fourth ventricle.
exam2.hint: Focus on the state of the vermis and whether the cyst opens into the fourth ventricle.

exam2.question: A neonate with a prenatally suspected midline anomaly has a coronal head sonogram showing widely separated, parallel frontal horns, a high-riding third ventricle, absent cavum septum pellucidum and dilated occipital horns. Midline sagittal scanning shows sulci radiating toward the third ventricle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Parallel lateral ventricles, colpocephaly, an elevated third ventricle and a radial (sunburst) sulcal pattern on midline sagittal views are classic for callosal agenesis. Aqueductal stenosis dilates the ventricles but preserves the corpus callosum and normal sulcal orientation.
exam2.hint: Look at the shape and spacing of the frontal horns and the orientation of the medial sulci on the sagittal view.

exam2.question: A newborn with an open lumbosacral myelomeningocele undergoes head ultrasound. Which posterior fossa finding is most expected?

options.text: An enlarged posterior fossa with cystic fourth ventricle
A large retrocerebellar cyst with an intact vermis
A normal posterior fossa with isolated cerebellar hypoplasia
A small posterior fossa with cerebellar tissue displaced through the foramen magnum

exam2.explanation: Open neural tube defects are associated with Chiari II malformation: a small posterior fossa, downward herniation of the vermis and brainstem, a beaked tectum and often hydrocephalus. An enlarged cystic posterior fossa describes the Dandy-Walker spectrum.
exam2.hint: Recall the hindbrain malformation that nearly always accompanies open spinal dysraphism.

exam2.question: A 25-week infant has a large intraventricular hemorrhage plus a fan-shaped echogenic area in the adjacent periventricular white matter extending toward the cortex. If this parenchymal lesion follows the usual course, what will it most likely become over the next several weeks?

options.text: A porencephalic cyst communicating with the lateral ventricle

exam2.explanation: Periventricular hemorrhagic infarction (grade IV) usually liquefies into a single porencephalic cavity that communicates with the ventricle. Multiple small bilateral cysts are typical of cystic PVL rather than hemorrhagic infarction.
exam2.hint: Think of how a single large area of hemorrhagic venous infarction resolves.

exam2.question: A 3-week-old with E. coli meningitis has a head sonogram showing an irregular, thickened echogenic ventricular lining, echogenic debris layering in the dependent ventricles and thin intraventricular strands. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: In a child with meningitis, a thickened irregular echogenic ependyma with intraventricular debris and septations indicates ventriculitis, which can progress to loculated hydrocephalus. Grade I hemorrhage is confined to the subependymal germinal matrix and does not line the ventricles.
exam2.hint: Relate the clinical history to the change in the ventricular walls and contents.

exam2.question: A 24-week infant has unexplained anemia, and cerebellar hemorrhage is suspected, but the posterior fossa is poorly seen through the anterior fontanelle. What is the most appropriate next step in the sonographic exam?

options.text: Increase depth through the anterior fontanelle
Scan through the temporal squamosa with a linear transducer
Obtain transcranial Doppler of the middle cerebral artery

exam2.explanation: The mastoid (posterolateral) fontanelle gives a close, axial view of the cerebellum and fourth ventricle and greatly improves detection of cerebellar hemorrhage. More depth through the anterior fontanelle still leaves the posterior fossa in the far field with poor resolution.
exam2.hint: Choose an acoustic window that sits closest to the cerebellum.

exam2.question: A dehydrated 10-day-old has seizures. Color and spectral Doppler through the anterior fontanelle, using a low velocity scale and light transducer pressure, show echogenic material filling the superior sagittal sinus with no detectable flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Echogenic intraluminal material with absent flow in the superior sagittal sinus, despite settings optimized for slow flow, indicates sinovenous thrombosis; dehydration is a major neonatal risk factor. Normal sinus flow is slow but detectable with a low scale, and heavy fontanelle pressure should be avoided because it can compress the sinus.
exam2.hint: Ask whether these settings would have detected normal slow venous flow.

exam2.question: A macrocephalic newborn has a cranium filled almost entirely with fluid. A falx is present, the thalami and brainstem are separate and intact, and no cerebral cortical mantle can be identified above them. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Hydranencephaly results from destruction of the anterior and middle cerebral artery territories, leaving fluid with a preserved falx, thalami and posterior fossa but no cortical mantle. Severe hydrocephalus still shows a thin rim of cortex surrounding the dilated ventricles.
exam2.hint: Distinguish a thinned cortical rim from complete absence of the cerebral mantle.

exam2.question: A term neonate develops high-output cardiac failure. Head ultrasound shows a midline anechoic tubular structure posterior to the third ventricle that fills with turbulent high-velocity flow on color Doppler and drains into a dilated straight sinus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A midline posterior cystic-appearing structure with turbulent arterialized flow, dilated draining sinuses and heart failure is a vein of Galen malformation. Arachnoid cysts and cavum velum interpositum are avascular on color Doppler.
exam2.hint: Let the color Doppler and the cardiac presentation separate a vascular lesion from simple fluid spaces.

exam2.question: A newborn has microcephaly, hepatosplenomegaly, petechiae and a failed hearing screen. Head ultrasound shows punctate echogenic foci with faint shadowing lining the lateral ventricles and branching linear echogenicities in the thalami. What is the most likely cause?
exam2.explanation: Periventricular calcifications with lenticulostriate vasculopathy, microcephaly, hepatosplenomegaly and sensorineural hearing loss are classic for congenital CMV. Toxoplasmosis calcifications tend to be scattered through the parenchyma and basal ganglia with hydrocephalus rather than predominantly periventricular.
exam2.hint: Match the periventricular distribution and hearing loss to the most common congenital infection.

exam2.question: An 8-month-old with an enlarging head circumference but normal development has widened anechoic extra-axial fluid over both frontal lobes. Color Doppler shows small cortical veins coursing through the fluid. Which interpretation is best supported?

options.text: Benign enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces

exam2.explanation: Vessels traversing the extra-axial fluid (cortical vein sign) place the fluid in the subarachnoid space, supporting benign enlargement in a macrocephalic infant. A subdural collection displaces the veins against the brain surface, so the veins do not cross it.
exam2.hint: Ask which compartment the cortical veins actually travel through.

exam2.question: On a coronal head sonogram of a preterm infant, which finding best favors germinal matrix hemorrhage over normal choroid plexus?

options.text: Echogenic tissue within the atrium of the lateral ventricle
An echogenic focus anterior to the caudothalamic groove in the frontal horn floor
Smooth echogenic tissue tapering toward the foramen of Monro
Symmetric echogenic tissue in both ventricular trigones

exam2.explanation: Choroid plexus does not extend into the frontal horn anterior to the caudothalamic groove, so echogenic material there indicates hemorrhage. Echogenic tissue in the atrium is the expected location of normal glomus choroid plexus.
exam2.hint: Use the anterior limit of normal choroid plexus as your landmark.

exam2.question: A 26-week infant has bilateral grade III intraventricular hemorrhage on day 4. What is the main reason serial head sonograms are scheduled over the following weeks?

options.text: To confirm resolution of physiologic choroid plexus cysts
To measure cortical sulcation for gestational age
To monitor closure of the anterior fontanelle

exam2.explanation: Post-hemorrhagic ventricular dilation commonly develops over the first few weeks after significant IVH and may require intervention, so serial ventricular measurements are needed. Fontanelle closure is months away and is not the reason for close follow-up.
exam2.hint: Consider the obstructive complication of blood products in the CSF pathways.

exam2.question: A term infant with seizures has a coronal head sonogram showing a fluid-filled cleft that extends from the lateral ventricle to the cortical surface and is lined by echogenic gray matter. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Schizencephaly is a transmantle cleft lined by gray matter that connects the ventricle with the subarachnoid space; in the open-lip form the cleft is filled with CSF. A porencephalic cavity results from destroyed tissue and is lined by white matter or gliosis rather than gray matter.
exam2.hint: Look at what tissue lines the cleft.

exam2.question: A 28-week infant had normal cranial ultrasounds in the first week of life. Why do many protocols repeat cranial sonography near term-equivalent age?

options.text: Germinal matrix hemorrhage usually begins after 36 weeks
The anterior fontanelle is too small to scan in the first week
Choroid plexus normally becomes visible only at term
Cystic white matter injury and ventriculomegaly may appear only weeks later

exam2.explanation: Early scans detect most germinal matrix hemorrhages, but cystic PVL and ventriculomegaly evolve over weeks and are best detected later. Most germinal matrix hemorrhages occur within the first days of life, not after 36 weeks.
exam2.hint: Think about which injuries have a delayed sonographic evolution.

exam2.question: A 5-week-old girl has persistent jaundice, direct hyperbilirubinemia and pale acholic stools. After a 4-hour fast, the gallbladder is small and irregular, and an echogenic band 5 mm thick lies anterior to the portal vein bifurcation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A thick echogenic triangular cord anterior to the portal bifurcation with an abnormal gallbladder in a cholestatic infant strongly suggests biliary atresia. Neonatal hepatitis can cause cholestasis but does not produce a thickened triangular cord.
exam2.hint: Focus on the fibrous remnant at the porta hepatis rather than the jaundice itself.

exam2.question: In the evaluation of a cholestatic infant, the triangular cord sign refers to echogenic fibrous tissue located where?

options.text: Anterior to the portal vein bifurcation at the porta hepatis
Within the gallbladder fossa replacing the gallbladder

exam2.explanation: The triangular cord is the fibrotic remnant of the extrahepatic bile duct seen just anterior to the portal vein bifurcation (commonly measured above the right portal vein, with about 4 mm as the most widely taught threshold). It is not measured in the gallbladder fossa or around hepatic veins.
exam2.hint: Picture where the obliterated common hepatic duct would normally run.

exam2.question: A 4-week-old is scheduled for ultrasound to evaluate prolonged conjugated jaundice. Why is the infant kept NPO for about 3 to 4 hours before the study?

options.text: To reduce bowel gas over the pancreas
To allow the liver to return to normal echogenicity
So a normal gallbladder will be distended and its absence or small size is meaningful

exam2.explanation: Fasting allows the gallbladder to fill, so a persistently small or absent gallbladder becomes a significant finding for biliary atresia. Bowel gas reduction is a secondary benefit and not the purpose in a cholestasis workup.
exam2.hint: Think about how feeding changes the size of a normal gallbladder.

exam2.question: Ultrasound and hepatobiliary scintigraphy in a 6-week-old strongly suggest biliary atresia. Which surgical treatment has the best outcome when performed early, ideally before about 2 months of age?
exam2.explanation: The Kasai procedure restores bile drainage from the porta hepatis to a jejunal limb, and success declines with age at surgery. Roux-en-Y cyst excision is the treatment for choledochal cyst, not biliary atresia.
exam2.hint: Recall the procedure that connects the porta hepatis directly to bowel.

exam2.question: An infant with biliary atresia has multiple small splenic masses in the left upper quadrant and a midline liver. Which associated vascular finding should the sonographer specifically look for?

options.text: Interrupted inferior vena cava with azygos continuation

exam2.explanation: The biliary atresia splenic malformation syndrome includes polysplenia, interrupted IVC with azygos continuation, preduodenal portal vein and situs anomalies. A persistent right umbilical vein is a fetal finding unrelated to this syndrome.
exam2.hint: Link polysplenia to the heterotaxy-related venous anomaly.

exam2.question: A 4-year-old girl has intermittent abdominal pain, mild jaundice and a palpable right upper quadrant mass. Ultrasound shows a 5 cm fusiform cystic structure in the porta hepatis that is separate from the gallbladder and in continuity with the common bile duct. Intrahepatic ducts are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Fusiform extrahepatic bile duct dilation connecting with the CBD and normal intrahepatic ducts is Todani type I, the most common choledochal cyst. A duplication cyst would show a gut-signature wall and no biliary communication.
exam2.hint: Confirm that the cyst is part of the bile duct itself.

exam2.question: A 4-year-old with 6 days of fever, conjunctival injection, a strawberry tongue and swollen hands has right upper quadrant pain. Ultrasound shows a markedly distended, thin-walled gallbladder with no stones, no wall thickening and no biliary dilation. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Acute gallbladder hydrops associated with Kawasaki disease

exam2.explanation: Kawasaki disease can cause acute acalculous distension (hydrops) of the gallbladder, which usually resolves as the vasculitis is treated. Calculous cholecystitis requires stones, and a choledochal cyst is a dilated bile duct rather than an enlarged gallbladder.
exam2.hint: Note what is absent from the gallbladder and the ducts, then explain the whole clinical picture.

exam2.question: An 18-month-old boy has an enlarging abdomen and a markedly elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein for age. Ultrasound shows a large heterogeneous solid mass in the right hepatic lobe with coarse calcifications and internal vascularity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Hepatoblastoma is the most common primary liver malignancy in children under 3 and typically presents as a solid, often calcified mass with high AFP. Mesenchymal hamartoma is predominantly cystic with normal AFP for age.
exam2.hint: Combine the patient age, the tumor marker and the solid nature of the mass.

exam2.question: Three days after liver transplantation, a 2-year-old has rising liver enzymes. Doppler shows normal portal venous and hepatic venous flow, but no arterial signal can be found at the porta hepatis or within the liver despite optimized settings. Which complication is most likely?
exam2.explanation: Absent hepatic arterial flow early after transplant indicates hepatic artery thrombosis, the most serious early vascular complication and more frequent in children because of small vessels; the transplanted bile ducts depend on arterial supply. Portal vein stenosis would show focal narrowing with aliasing and poststenotic turbulence.
exam2.hint: Work out which of the inflow and outflow vessels is missing a signal.

exam2.question: A 12-year-old with cirrhosis from autoimmune hepatitis has splenomegaly. A vessel within the ligamentum teres carries flow from the left portal vein toward the umbilicus. What does this finding indicate?

options.text: Portal hypertension with a recanalized paraumbilical vein

exam2.explanation: A recanalized paraumbilical vein arising from the left portal vein and draining toward the abdominal wall is a portosystemic collateral that indicates portal hypertension of intrahepatic or posthepatic origin. The ductus venosus connects the portal sinus with the IVC and normally closes in the first weeks of life.
exam2.hint: Consider what pressure gradient would push portal blood out along the ligamentum teres.

exam2.question: A 3-year-old with fatigue and fever has a spleen measuring 12 cm in length. How should this measurement be interpreted?

options.text: Normal only if the child is male

exam2.explanation: Pediatric splenic length is age-dependent; commonly used references place the upper limit for a toddler at roughly 8 to 9 cm, so 12 cm is splenomegaly. Adult-size values near 12 cm are not normal in a 3-year-old.
exam2.hint: Normal splenic length increases with age; estimate the expected upper limit for a preschool child before deciding.

exam2.question: A preterm infant has an umbilical venous catheter placed. On ultrasound, where should the catheter tip ideally lie?

options.text: At or near the junction of the IVC and right atrium

exam2.explanation: The UVC passes from the umbilical vein through the left portal vein and ductus venosus into the IVC, and its tip should lie at or near the IVC-right atrial junction. A tip left in the portal system risks portal vein thrombosis and hepatic injury from infused fluids.
exam2.hint: Trace the fetal venous pathway the catheter follows and decide where it should end.

exam2.question: A 6-year-old struck the epigastrium on bicycle handlebars and now has epigastric pain and elevated lipase. Ultrasound shows a hypoechoic cleft through the pancreas with fluid in the lesser sac. Where is a traumatic pancreatic injury most likely located?

options.text: At the tail near the splenic hilum
At the uncinate process behind the SMV
At the neck or body where the pancreas crosses the spine
At the head within the duodenal C-loop

exam2.explanation: Blunt epigastric force compresses the pancreatic neck and body against the vertebral column, the classic site of transection. The tail is mobile and less often crushed against bone.
exam2.hint: Picture which part of the gland lies directly on a rigid structure.

exam2.question: A hemodynamically stable 8-year-old has a focused abdominal sonogram after falling from a tree. No free fluid is seen. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Solid organ injury can occur without free fluid, so CT is used if suspicion persists
A negative study excludes solid organ injury
Free fluid is only visible once it exceeds 1 liter
This study is more sensitive than CT for splenic laceration

exam2.explanation: In children, many solid organ injuries occur without hemoperitoneum, so a negative focused sonogram does not exclude injury, and contrast CT remains the reference standard for a stable child with ongoing concern. Sonography is much less sensitive than CT for parenchymal lacerations.
exam2.hint: Ask whether every solid organ laceration bleeds into the peritoneal cavity.

exam2.question: A 6-year-old receiving L-asparaginase for acute lymphoblastic leukemia develops severe epigastric pain and a markedly raised lipase. Which ultrasound appearance is most expected?

options.text: Small, echogenic pancreas from fatty replacement
Enlarged, hypoechoic pancreas with peripancreatic fluid
Normal pancreas with a dilated duct from stones
Atrophic gland with multiple coarse calcifications

exam2.explanation: Asparaginase is a well-known cause of acute pancreatitis in children, which appears as an enlarged hypoechoic gland with peripancreatic fluid, although the pancreas can look normal early. A small echogenic gland reflects chronic fatty replacement, as in cystic fibrosis, and coarse calcifications indicate chronic pancreatitis.
exam2.hint: Decide whether this drug reaction produces an acute or a chronic pancreatic process, then recall how each changes the gland.

exam2.question: A 9-year-old with glycogen storage disease type I has hepatomegaly with diffusely increased echogenicity. On surveillance ultrasound, which lesion is this child at increased risk of developing?
exam2.explanation: Glycogen storage disease type I predisposes to hepatic adenomas, which can bleed or rarely transform, so periodic imaging is performed. Infantile hemangioma and mesenchymal hamartoma are lesions of infancy unrelated to GSD.
exam2.hint: Consider which of these lesions arise in infancy and which develop later in a child with this metabolic disorder.

exam2.question: A 7-year-old has intermittent abdominal pain and now constant severe pain. No spleen is seen in the left upper quadrant. A large homogeneous hypoechoic organ-shaped mass lies in the lower abdomen with a whirled vascular pedicle and no internal color flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: An absent spleen in its normal location plus an ectopic splenic-shaped mass with a twisted pedicle and no flow indicates torsion of a wandering spleen. Omental infarction is a triangular echogenic fat mass, not an organ-shaped hypoechoic structure.
exam2.hint: Start with what is missing from the left upper quadrant.

exam2.question: A 10-year-old with sickle cell disease has right upper quadrant pain. Ultrasound shows multiple small mobile shadowing echogenic foci in the gallbladder. What is the main reason gallstones form in this patient?

options.text: Bacterial infection of the bile ducts

exam2.explanation: Ongoing hemolysis raises the bilirubin load, producing calcium bilirubinate pigment stones in children with sickle cell disease. Cholesterol stones are typical of obesity-related cholelithiasis in adolescents.
exam2.hint: Think about the breakdown product released when red cells are destroyed.

exam2.question: A 10-year-old treated with chemotherapy for neuroblastoma in infancy has an incidental, well-defined, mildly hypoechoic liver mass with a central scar. Color Doppler shows a central feeding artery with vessels radiating outward. Alpha-fetoprotein is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A central scar with a spoke-wheel arterial pattern is typical of focal nodular hyperplasia, which occurs with increased frequency in children after chemotherapy or radiation. Hepatoblastoma occurs in younger children and is associated with markedly raised AFP.
exam2.hint: Focus on the pattern of the vessels radiating from the center.

exam2.question: A 5-week-old boy has progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting and a palpable epigastric olive. The pyloric muscle wall measures 4.5 mm, the channel length is 19 mm, and no gastric fluid passes through the canal during 10 minutes of observation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A single muscle wall thickness of 3 mm or more and a channel length of about 15 mm or more (most widely taught cutoffs) with failure of fluid passage diagnose HPS. Pylorospasm produces transient thickening that relaxes and allows passage.
exam2.hint: Compare each measurement with the commonly taught thresholds and note fluid passage.

exam2.question: A 3-week-old with intermittent vomiting has a pyloric muscle thickness of 2.2 mm. Over 10 minutes, the channel length and wall thickness change, and fluid eventually passes into the duodenum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Variable pyloric measurements that normalize and allow fluid passage indicate pylorospasm, which is transient and managed conservatively. HPS shows persistent thickening of about 3 mm or more without opening.
exam2.hint: Persistence over time is the key distinction between muscle hypertrophy and spasm.

exam2.question: A 6-week-old with sonographically confirmed hypertrophic pyloric stenosis has been vomiting for several days. Which laboratory pattern is most expected?
exam2.explanation: Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid through vomiting produces a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis that must be corrected before pyloromyotomy. Acidosis would suggest bowel ischemia or sepsis rather than isolated gastric outlet obstruction.
exam2.hint: Think about which ions are lost in pure gastric contents.

exam2.question: A 9-month-old boy has episodes of inconsolable crying with drawing up of the legs and a red currant-jelly stool. A 3.5 cm mass in the right upper quadrant shows concentric alternating hypoechoic and echogenic rings in transverse section and a reniform appearance longitudinally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A target appearance about 3 cm or larger in the right abdomen in a 6- to 36-month-old with colicky pain and bloody stool is classic ileocolic intussusception. Small-bowel intussusceptions are smaller (usually under 2.5 cm) and often transient.
exam2.hint: Use the mass size, location and patient age together.

exam2.question: During ultrasound-guided saline enema reduction of an ileocolic intussusception, which finding best confirms complete reduction?

options.text: The mass moves back toward the hepatic flexure
Peristalsis is seen in the transverse colon
The mass disappears and saline flows freely into the terminal ileum

exam2.explanation: Reduction is complete when the intussusceptum is no longer seen and fluid passes freely through the ileocecal valve, distending the terminal ileum. Retrograde movement of the mass alone is only partial reduction, and an edematous ileocecal valve can mimic residual intussusception.
exam2.hint: Partial reduction can look encouraging; decide which observation cannot occur until the intussusceptum is completely out of the colon.

exam2.question: Compared with a typical 9-month-old, a 7-year-old with ileocolic intussusception is more likely to have which finding?

options.text: Idiopathic lymphoid hyperplasia as the only cause
A pathologic lead point such as lymphoma
An intussusception confined to the jejunum

exam2.explanation: Most intussusceptions in infants are idiopathic, but beyond about 5 years a pathologic lead point (Burkitt lymphoma, Meckel diverticulum, polyp) becomes more likely. Idiopathic lymphoid hyperplasia is the typical mechanism in infants.
exam2.hint: Consider how the cause of intussusception shifts with age.

exam2.question: Which finding is an absolute contraindication to enema reduction of an ileocolic intussusception?

options.text: A small amount of simple free fluid

exam2.explanation: Peritonitis, pneumoperitoneum from perforation and hemodynamic shock are absolute contraindications, and these children go to surgery. Longer symptom duration and lymph nodes within the mass lower success rates but do not by themselves prevent an attempt.
exam2.hint: Separate factors that lower the success rate from those that make an attempt unsafe.

exam2.question: An 11-year-old girl has 24 hours of periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, fever and leukocytosis. Graded compression shows a noncompressible blind-ending tubular structure measuring 8 mm in outer diameter, surrounded by echogenic fat, with a shadowing echogenic focus in the lumen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A noncompressible appendix greater than 6 mm with inflamed periappendiceal fat and an appendicolith is diagnostic of acute appendicitis. Mesenteric adenitis requires a normal appendix.
exam2.hint: Apply the diameter and compressibility criteria to the blind-ending structure.

exam2.question: A 7-year-old with 4 days of right lower quadrant pain has an appendix with circumferential loss of the echogenic submucosal layer and an adjacent complex loculated fluid collection. What do these findings most likely indicate?
exam2.explanation: Loss of the echogenic submucosa and a loculated periappendiceal collection indicate perforation and abscess formation, often after several days of symptoms. Early appendicitis preserves the submucosal layer.
exam2.hint: Consider which wall layer is lost once the appendix ruptures.

exam2.question: An overweight 8-year-old has 3 days of right-sided abdominal pain without fever. Ultrasound shows a normal compressible appendix and an ovoid, noncompressible hyperechoic fatty mass beneath the anterior abdominal wall at the point of maximal tenderness, with little internal flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A tender, noncompressible echogenic fat mass adjacent to the abdominal wall with a normal appendix is typical of omental infarction, which is usually managed conservatively. Mesenteric adenitis shows clusters of enlarged nodes rather than an infarcted fat mass.
exam2.hint: Identify which tissue is echogenic and noncompressible at the point of tenderness.

exam2.question: A 10-day-old has sudden bilious vomiting. Ultrasound shows a dilated, fluid-filled proximal duodenum, the superior mesenteric vein lying to the left of the superior mesenteric artery, and the SMV and mesentery wrapping clockwise around the SMA when scanning caudally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: An inverted SMA/SMV relationship with a clockwise whirlpool sign and duodenal obstruction in a neonate with bilious vomiting indicates midgut volvulus, a surgical emergency. Pyloric stenosis causes nonbilious vomiting.
exam2.hint: Bilious vomiting in a newborn plus a twisted mesentery is the key combination.

exam2.question: A 9-year-old with leukemia and profound neutropenia after chemotherapy has fever and right lower quadrant pain. Ultrasound shows a normal appendix and marked circumferential wall thickening of the cecum and ascending colon with surrounding inflamed fat. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Neutropenic enterocolitis is a necrotizing inflammation centered on the cecum and right colon in profoundly neutropenic patients, seen as marked bowel wall thickening. Crohn disease follows a chronic course and usually involves the terminal ileum.
exam2.hint: Combine the immune status with the segment of bowel involved.

exam2.question: A 15-year-old with weight loss, diarrhea and right lower quadrant pain has a 7 mm thick, hyperemic terminal ileal wall with loss of layering and surrounding echogenic, mass-like mesenteric fat that separates bowel loops. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Infectious colitis limited to the cecum

exam2.explanation: Transmural terminal ileal thickening with hyperemia and fibrofatty mesenteric proliferation (creeping fat) is typical of Crohn disease. Ulcerative colitis involves the colon continuously from the rectum and spares the terminal ileum apart from backwash.
exam2.hint: The segment involved and the fat changes point to a transmural process.

exam2.question: A newborn has abdominal distension. Ultrasound shows scattered shadowing echogenic foci along the peritoneal surfaces and liver capsule and a thick-walled cystic collection with echogenic contents. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Meconium peritonitis from in utero bowel perforation

exam2.explanation: Bowel perforation in utero spills meconium into the peritoneum, causing chemical peritonitis with peritoneal calcifications and sometimes a walled-off meconium pseudocyst. NEC causes intramural and portal venous gas after birth, mainly in preterm infants, not calcified peritoneal plaques at birth.
exam2.hint: Note where the calcifications lie and when the process must have begun.

exam2.question: A preterm infant with known necrotizing enterocolitis is rescanned. Which finding most suggests disease progression that may require surgery?

options.text: Complex ascites with echoes and focal fluid collections
Mildly thickened bowel wall with increased flow
Small amount of anechoic free fluid

exam2.explanation: Complex echogenic ascites or loculated collections suggest perforation and are associated with need for surgery. Mild wall thickening with hyperemia reflects inflammation of viable bowel.
exam2.hint: Ask which fluid quality signals bowel contents or pus in the peritoneum.

exam2.question: A distended neonate is scanned supine. An echogenic line with posterior reverberation artifacts lies between the anterior abdominal wall and the liver surface and obscures the underlying liver. What does this most likely indicate?
exam2.explanation: Free air rises to the nondependent anterior abdomen in a supine infant and appears as an enhanced peritoneal stripe with reverberation between the liver and abdominal wall, indicating perforation. Portal venous gas appears as moving echogenic foci within portal veins and branching echoes in the liver.
exam2.hint: Consider where gas collects in a supine baby and whether it is inside or outside bowel.

exam2.question: A 2-year-old boy has painless, large-volume bright red rectal bleeding. Abdominal ultrasound is unrevealing. Which next imaging study is most specific for the likely cause?
exam2.explanation: Painless rectal bleeding in a toddler suggests a Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa, which takes up pertechnetate. Hepatobiliary scintigraphy evaluates bile flow, not gastric mucosa.
exam2.hint: Think about the ectopic tissue type that causes the bleeding and what tracer it concentrates.

exam2.question: A 6-year-old has palpable purpura on the legs, arthralgia and colicky abdominal pain. Ultrasound shows segmental jejunal and ileal wall thickening with intramural hemorrhage. Which complication should the sonographer specifically look for?
exam2.explanation: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) causes intramural bowel hemorrhage that can act as a lead point for small-bowel (ileoileal) intussusception. Pyloric stenosis and biliary atresia occur in young infants.
exam2.hint: Consider the complication that focal small-bowel wall thickening can trigger in this disease.

exam2.question: A newborn with trisomy 21 has vomiting shortly after birth. Ultrasound shows a fluid-distended stomach and proximal duodenum with no fluid or gas in more distal bowel. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: The double bubble with no distal bowel content is typical of duodenal atresia, strongly associated with trisomy 21. Pyloric stenosis presents weeks after birth and does not distend the duodenum.
exam2.hint: Recall which congenital obstruction pairs with Down syndrome and two fluid-filled bubbles.

exam2.question: A 12-year-old with flank pain has a 4 mm echogenic focus in the lower pole collecting system without definite shadowing. On color Doppler, a rapidly changing mix of colors appears directly behind the focus. What does this finding most likely indicate?

options.text: A urinary stone producing twinkling artifact

exam2.explanation: Twinkling artifact, a rapidly alternating color signal deep to a rough reflective surface, increases sensitivity for small urinary stones that may not shadow. Aneurysms and fistulas show true flow with characteristic spectral waveforms rather than noise behind an echogenic focus.
exam2.hint: Consider how a rough, strongly reflective surface can affect the color Doppler display.

exam2.question: A 2-week-old has clear fluid draining from the umbilicus that increases with crying. Ultrasound shows a tubular fluid-filled tract running from the bladder dome along the anterior abdominal wall to the umbilicus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A tract connecting the bladder dome with the umbilicus that leaks urine is a patent urachus, the fully open form of urachal remnant. A urachal cyst is a closed collection along the tract that does not drain, and an omphalomesenteric remnant connects the umbilicus with the ileum.
exam2.hint: Identify the organ at the deep end of the tract.

exam2.question: A 2-month-old boy with prenatally detected left hydronephrosis has marked pelvicaliectasis with an abruptly tapering renal pelvis. The ureter is not visualized, and the bladder is normal. Which study is most appropriate next to assess for functional obstruction?
exam2.explanation: Findings suggest ureteropelvic junction obstruction, and diuretic renography (for example MAG3 with furosemide) quantifies split function and drainage. Hepatobiliary scintigraphy assesses bile excretion, not urinary drainage.
exam2.hint: Choose a test that measures both kidney function and urine drainage.

exam2.question: A 7-year-old girl with Turner syndrome has kidneys whose lower poles are medially oriented and joined by a band of renal parenchyma crossing anterior to the aorta. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Fusion of the lower poles by an isthmus anterior to the aorta is a horseshoe kidney, common in Turner syndrome and associated with UPJ obstruction, stones and an increased risk of Wilms tumor. In crossed fused ectopia both kidneys lie on the same side of the midline.
exam2.hint: Note where the bridging tissue lies relative to the great vessels.

exam2.question: A 1-week-old boy with posterior urethral valves has kidneys that are small with markedly increased cortical echogenicity, poor corticomedullary differentiation and several small subcortical cysts. What do these findings most likely represent?
exam2.explanation: Early in utero obstruction can cause renal dysplasia, appearing as echogenic kidneys with poor differentiation and cortical cysts, a predictor of poor renal function. Normal neonatal kidneys have prominent hypoechoic pyramids and no cysts.
exam2.hint: Think about what chronic fetal obstruction does to developing nephrons.

exam2.question: A newborn has a palpable left flank mass. Ultrasound shows multiple anechoic cysts of varying size that do not connect with each other, no central renal pelvis and no recognizable renal parenchyma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Noncommunicating cysts of different sizes replacing the kidney with no pelvis or functioning parenchyma define MCDK. In severe UPJ obstruction the dilated calyces all connect to a central dilated pelvis.
exam2.hint: Test whether the fluid spaces connect to a central collecting structure.

exam2.question: An infant has a confirmed left multicystic dysplastic kidney. Why is careful evaluation of the right kidney essential?

options.text: The right kidney is usually absent
Contralateral anomalies such as reflux or UPJ obstruction are common
The right kidney is the usual site of Wilms tumor in MCDK

exam2.explanation: Because the MCDK is nonfunctioning, renal function depends on the contralateral kidney, which has a high rate of anomalies, most commonly vesicoureteral reflux and UPJ obstruction. The contralateral kidney typically shows compensatory hypertrophy, not absence.
exam2.hint: Remember the patient relies entirely on one kidney.

exam2.question: A newborn with a history of oligohydramnios has respiratory distress. Both kidneys are markedly enlarged and diffusely echogenic with loss of corticomedullary differentiation and innumerable tiny cysts. The parents have normal renal ultrasounds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Bilaterally enlarged echogenic kidneys from dilated collecting tubules, oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia with normal parents fit ARPKD. ADPKD would usually show cysts in an affected parent.
exam2.hint: Use the inheritance clue from the parents along with bilateral symmetric involvement.

exam2.question: A 9-year-old with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease has splenomegaly and esophageal varices. Which liver abnormality most likely explains these findings?
exam2.explanation: ARPKD is accompanied by congenital hepatic fibrosis, which causes portal hypertension that predominates in older survivors. Budd-Chiari is a hepatic venous outflow obstruction unrelated to ARPKD.
exam2.hint: Recall the inverse relationship between renal and hepatic disease severity in ARPKD.

exam2.question: A 6-year-old girl with a repaired lumbar myelomeningocele has recurrent urinary tract infections. Ultrasound shows a thick-walled, irregular, trabeculated bladder with several small diverticula, bilateral hydroureteronephrosis and a large postvoid residual. What is the most likely cause?
exam2.explanation: Spinal dysraphism disrupts bladder innervation, causing a high-pressure neurogenic bladder with wall thickening, trabeculation, diverticula, poor emptying and upper tract dilation. Posterior urethral valves occur only in boys and show a dilated posterior urethra.
exam2.hint: Connect the spinal history to how the bladder empties and the pressure it generates.

exam2.question: A 2-year-old with hemihypertrophy undergoes surveillance ultrasound. Both kidneys are enlarged with a thick, homogeneous, solid hypoechoic subcapsular rind. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Nephrogenic rests can form a diffuse hypoechoic peripheral rind (diffuse hyperplastic perilobar nephroblastomatosis), a Wilms tumor precursor seen in overgrowth syndromes such as hemihypertrophy and Beckwith-Wiedemann. ARPKD enlarges the kidneys with diffusely increased echogenicity rather than a hypoechoic rind.
exam2.hint: Consider why a child with an overgrowth syndrome is being screened in the first place.

exam2.question: A 4-month-old has massive hepatomegaly with innumerable small hypoechoic liver nodules, a small right adrenal mass and bluish skin nodules. Bone marrow involvement is minimal. Which statement about this condition is most accurate?

options.text: It is stage MS neuroblastoma, which often regresses spontaneously
It is metastatic Wilms tumor with a poor prognosis
It is infantile hepatic hemangioma with adrenal hemorrhage
It is hepatoblastoma with adrenal metastasis

exam2.explanation: Infants under 18 months with metastases limited to liver, skin and minimal marrow have stage MS (formerly 4S) neuroblastoma, which carries a favorable prognosis and can regress. Wilms tumor rarely metastasizes to skin.
exam2.hint: Note the patient age and the specific sites of spread: liver, skin and limited marrow.

exam2.question: A 3-year-old with bloody diarrhea, anemia, thrombocytopenia and oliguria has enlarged echogenic kidneys, and intrarenal arterial Doppler shows absent diastolic flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Hemolytic uremic syndrome after Shiga toxin-producing E. coli causes acute kidney injury with echogenic kidneys and reduced or absent intrarenal diastolic flow; return of diastolic flow often precedes recovery of urine output. Renal vein thrombosis typically presents in neonates with a flank mass and hematuria.
exam2.hint: Link the diarrheal prodrome with the blood count findings.

exam2.question: A girl with a duplex right kidney has a dilated upper pole collecting system and an ectopic ureterocele in the bladder. Per the Weigert-Meyer rule, which moiety is most likely to have vesicoureteral reflux?

options.text: Neither moiety, because duplex systems cannot reflux

exam2.explanation: The upper pole ureter inserts ectopically, inferomedially, and tends to obstruct with a ureterocele, whereas the lower pole ureter inserts laterally with a short tunnel and tends to reflux. Obstruction is the usual problem for the upper moiety.
exam2.hint: Think about which ureteral orifice is displaced laterally with a short submucosal tunnel.

exam2.question: A 12-year-old with tuberous sclerosis has multiple well-defined, markedly hyperechoic masses in both kidneys, the largest 2 cm. What are these lesions most likely to be?
exam2.explanation: Multiple bilateral echogenic fat-containing angiomyolipomas, often with renal cysts, are characteristic of tuberous sclerosis; larger lesions risk hemorrhage. Wilms tumors are usually iso- to hypoechoic solid masses and are not typical of tuberous sclerosis.
exam2.hint: Ask which tissue component makes a renal lesion markedly echogenic.

exam2.question: A 2-year-old with a febrile urinary tract infection has a normal renal ultrasound. Which study is considered the reference standard for detecting acute pyelonephritis and later renal scarring?
exam2.explanation: DMSA binds functioning proximal tubular cells, so areas of pyelonephritis or scar appear as photopenic defects; it is the reference standard for parenchymal involvement. VCUG detects reflux but does not image parenchymal injury.
exam2.hint: Decide whether the question asks about urine flow or about the renal parenchyma itself.

exam2.question: A 3-year-old girl with recurrent febrile UTIs needs evaluation for vesicoureteral reflux, and the family wants to avoid ionizing radiation. Which ultrasound-based examination is most appropriate?

options.text: Color Doppler of ureteral jets alone

exam2.explanation: Contrast-enhanced voiding urosonography uses intravesical ultrasound contrast to detect and grade reflux without radiation and is an accepted alternative to VCUG. Ureteral jets and renal length cannot reliably detect reflux.
exam2.hint: Reflux is a dynamic event; choose the study that can actually show it happening without x-rays.

exam2.question: A 10-year-old with neurofibromatosis type 1 has severe hypertension. Intrarenal arterial waveforms in the right kidney show a delayed systolic upstroke with a rounded, low-amplitude peak; the left kidney is normal. What is the most likely cause?
exam2.explanation: A tardus parvus intrarenal waveform reflects an upstream arterial stenosis; renovascular hypertension in children is often due to NF1 vasculopathy or fibromuscular dysplasia. Renal vein thrombosis produces absent venous flow with high-resistance or reversed arterial diastolic flow.
exam2.hint: Ask what a narrowing upstream does to the shape of a downstream arterial waveform.

exam2.question: A 6-year-old has a bladder ultrasound for voiding dysfunction. Using the commonly taught Koff formula, what is the expected bladder capacity?
exam2.explanation: Expected bladder capacity in children is commonly estimated as (age in years + 2) x 30 mL, which is about 240 mL for a 6-year-old; this helps judge whether a prevoid bladder is adequately filled. 360 mL or more approaches adult capacity.
exam2.hint: Recall the age-based capacity estimate used for children up to about 12 years.

exam2.question: A 13-year-old boy has a right-sided varicocele that does not decompress when he lies supine; the left side is normal. What additional evaluation is most appropriate?

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound for a retroperitoneal mass or IVC obstruction

exam2.explanation: Left varicoceles are common because the left gonadal vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein; an isolated right or nondecompressing varicocele raises concern for a retroperitoneal or renal mass or IVC obstruction. Isolated left varicoceles in adolescents are usually idiopathic.
exam2.hint: Consider why varicoceles usually occur on the left side.

exam2.question: A 6-year-old girl has breast development and a growth spurt. Pelvic ultrasound shows a pear-shaped uterus with the fundus larger than the cervix, a visible endometrial stripe, and ovaries with several follicles bilaterally. What is the most likely interpretation?

options.text: Pubertal-appearing uterus consistent with precocious puberty

exam2.explanation: A prepubertal uterus is tubular with cervix equal to or larger than the fundus; a pear shape with an endometrial echo indicates estrogen stimulation, supporting precocious puberty. Mullerian agenesis would show no uterus.
exam2.hint: Compare fundus-to-cervix proportions before and after puberty.

exam2.question: A 12-year-old boy has a painless, firm testicular nodule. Ultrasound shows a well-circumscribed, avascular intratesticular mass with alternating concentric hypoechoic and echogenic rings. Tumor markers are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: An avascular, well-defined intratesticular mass with an onion-ring pattern of laminated keratin is typical of an epidermoid cyst, a benign lesion that may allow testis-sparing surgery. Yolk sac tumors are vascular solid masses with elevated AFP.
exam2.hint: Focus on the internal layering and the absence of flow.

exam2.question: A 12-year-old girl with acute pelvic pain has a torsed left ovary containing an echogenic mass with posterior shadowing that obscures its back wall, a fat-fluid level and an echogenic nodule projecting into the cyst. What is the most likely lesion?
exam2.explanation: The tip-of-the-iceberg shadowing, fat-fluid level and dermoid plug are typical of a mature cystic teratoma, the most common ovarian neoplasm in children and a frequent lead point for torsion. Endometriomas show homogeneous low-level echoes without fat.
exam2.hint: Look for the components that indicate fat and hair.

exam2.question: A 15-year-old girl has sudden pelvic pain in mid-cycle. The right ovary contains a 3 cm cyst with a fine lacy reticular internal pattern and no internal color flow; the surrounding ovarian tissue has normal flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A lacy or fishnet reticular pattern without internal flow reflects fibrin strands in a hemorrhagic cyst, which usually resolves on follow-up. A dermoid shows echogenic fat, shadowing and a fat-fluid level, and torsion produces an enlarged ovary with peripheral follicles.
exam2.hint: Focus on the internal pattern and whether it contains flow.

exam2.question: A 14-year-old girl with regular menses has worsening cyclic pelvic pain. Ultrasound shows two separate uterine horns with two cervices, a distended right hemivagina filled with low-level echoes, and no kidney in the right renal fossa. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Obstructed hemivagina with ipsilateral renal agenesis

exam2.explanation: Uterine didelphys with an obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral renal agenesis (OHVIRA, Herlyn-Werner-Wunderlich) explains cyclic pain despite normal menstruation from the unobstructed side. An imperforate hymen causes primary amenorrhea.
exam2.hint: Explain why menses are normal even though there is an obstructed collection.

exam2.question: A 2-day-old girl had a fetal ovarian cyst. Postnatal ultrasound shows a 5 cm pelvic-abdominal cyst with a fluid-debris level and a retracting echogenic clot. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Hemorrhage, often due to torsion, within a neonatal ovarian cyst
Simple follicular cyst expected to regress

exam2.explanation: A fluid-debris level or retracting clot in a neonatal ovarian cyst indicates hemorrhage, most often from torsion, and these cysts are less likely to resolve. A simple cyst would be anechoic.
exam2.hint: Interpret what internal debris and clot mean in a previously simple cyst.

exam2.question: A 14-year-old boy has 4 hours of sudden severe left scrotal pain and nausea, with an absent cremasteric reflex. The left testis is enlarged and hypoechoic with no intratesticular color flow, and a twisted spermatic cord is seen above the testis. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Antibiotics and repeat scan in 48 hours

exam2.explanation: Absent flow with a twisted cord confirms testicular torsion, a surgical emergency in which salvage depends on rapid detorsion. Antibiotics are appropriate for epididymitis, which shows increased flow.
exam2.hint: Time to treatment determines whether the testis survives.

exam2.question: In acute testicular torsion, which factor most strongly predicts testicular salvage?
exam2.explanation: Salvage rates are highest when detorsion occurs within about 6 hours and fall sharply thereafter. Hydrocele size and laterality do not determine viability.
exam2.hint: Think of the clock rather than the anatomy.

exam2.question: A 2-month-old girl has a firm, nontender labial swelling. Ultrasound shows a small ovoid structure containing tiny follicles, with internal color flow, within the inguinal canal. What is the most likely finding?

options.text: Hydrocele of the canal of Nuck

exam2.explanation: An ovoid structure with small follicles in the inguinal canal of an infant girl is a herniated ovary, which needs prompt repair because of incarceration and torsion risk; documenting its blood flow is important. A canal of Nuck hydrocele is a simple fluid collection without follicles.
exam2.hint: Look closely at the internal architecture of the structure.

exam2.question: A 5-year-old boy has a second episode of acute epididymitis with an enlarged hyperemic epididymis. Because epididymitis is uncommon at this age, which additional evaluation is most appropriate?

options.text: Serum alpha-fetoprotein for germ cell tumor
Assessment for an underlying urinary tract anomaly

exam2.explanation: Recurrent epididymitis in prepubertal boys often relates to urinary tract anomalies such as an ectopic ureter inserting into the seminal vesicle or vas, or voiding dysfunction. Tumor markers are not indicated for an inflammatory process.
exam2.hint: Consider why an uncommon infection would keep recurring in a young boy.

exam2.question: A newborn boy has a firm, painless, discolored scrotal mass present at birth. The testis is enlarged and heterogeneous with a thin echogenic peripheral rim and no internal color flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Perinatal torsion is extravaginal, involves the whole cord and tunica, and usually presents as a painless firm mass with an avascular heterogeneous testis and peripheral echogenic rim. A hydrocele surrounds a normal testis with normal flow.
exam2.hint: Note that the event likely happened before or around birth.

exam2.question: A 7-year-old boy has precocious puberty with a high testosterone and suppressed gonadotropins. Scrotal ultrasound shows a small, well-defined hypoechoic intratesticular nodule with increased vascularity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A small hypoechoic hypervascular intratesticular mass in a boy with gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty suggests a testosterone-secreting Leydig cell tumor. Epidermoid cysts are avascular and hormonally inactive.
exam2.hint: Ask whether the hormone excess begins in the pituitary or in the testis.

exam2.question: A newborn with ambiguous genitalia has salt-wasting and a raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Pelvic ultrasound shows a uterus behind the bladder, and the adrenal glands are enlarged with a cerebriform pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia in a 46,XX infant

exam2.explanation: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency virilizes 46,XX infants, who keep normal Mullerian structures including a uterus; the adrenals are often enlarged with a wrinkled cerebriform appearance. In androgen insensitivity, anti-Mullerian hormone from the testes prevents uterine development.
exam2.hint: Ask what the presence of a uterus implies about anti-Mullerian hormone.

exam2.question: A 3-month-old has an irreducible, tender right inguinal mass and vomiting. Ultrasound shows a fluid-filled bowel loop with thickened wall and no peristalsis in the inguinal canal, with free fluid in the sac. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Bowel within the inguinal canal that cannot be reduced, with wall thickening and absent peristalsis, indicates incarceration with risk of strangulation. An encysted cord hydrocele is a simple fluid collection without bowel wall.
exam2.hint: Identify the gut-wall structure and its lack of motion.

exam2.question: A 14-year-old girl, 1 year after menarche, has irregular menses. Transabdominal ultrasound shows ovaries with numerous small peripheral follicles. How should this finding be used?

options.text: It is common at this age and is not used to diagnose PCOS this soon after menarche
It is diagnostic of polycystic ovary syndrome on its own
It indicates ovarian hyperstimulation needing urgent treatment

exam2.explanation: Multifollicular ovaries are common in normal adolescents, so the 2018 and 2023 international PCOS guidelines advise against using ovarian ultrasound to diagnose PCOS within 8 years of menarche; diagnosis relies on irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism. Torsion causes a painful enlarged ovary, usually unilateral.
exam2.hint: Consider how a normal pubertal ovary looks.

exam2.question: A 9-year-old boy with acute lymphoblastic leukemia in bone marrow remission has painless bilateral scrotal enlargement. Both testes are diffusely enlarged and hypoechoic with markedly increased flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: The testis is a sanctuary site for leukemia relapse, appearing as diffuse or nodular hypoechoic hypervascular enlargement, often bilateral and painless. Orchitis would usually be painful.
exam2.hint: Weigh the painless, bilateral presentation alongside the oncologic history.

exam2.question: A 12-year-old boy with poorly controlled congenital adrenal hyperplasia has bilateral, eccentric hypoechoic lesions near the mediastinum testis with mild vascularity. Tumor markers are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Tubular ectasia of the rete testis

exam2.explanation: Elevated ACTH in congenital adrenal hyperplasia stimulates adrenal rest cells near the mediastinum testis, producing bilateral hypoechoic lesions that can regress with steroid therapy. Seminoma is rare in this age group and usually unilateral.
exam2.hint: Consider why the lesions are bilateral and clustered near the mediastinum testis in this endocrine disorder.

exam2.question: A 15-year-old boy was kicked in the scrotum during soccer. Which sonographic finding most specifically indicates testicular rupture requiring surgery?

options.text: Discontinuity of the tunica albuginea with irregular testicular contour

exam2.explanation: A breach in the echogenic tunica albuginea with contour deformity and heterogeneous parenchyma indicates rupture, which needs prompt repair. Wall thickening and small hydroceles are nonspecific after trauma.
exam2.hint: Focus on the integrity of the testicular capsule.

exam2.question: A 1-month-old has a dimple 3 cm above the gluteal cleft with intermittent discharge. Spinal ultrasound shows a thin hypoechoic tract extending from the skin through the subcutaneous fat toward the spinal canal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A tract running from a high midline dimple deep toward the dura is a dorsal dermal sinus, which can cause meningitis or harbor a dermoid and needs MRI and surgical excision. A coccygeal pit lies low within the gluteal cleft and ends blindly near the coccyx.
exam2.hint: Note the height of the dimple and where its tract ends.

exam2.question: A newborn with a lumbar hairy patch has a spinal ultrasound showing two hemicords in the lower thoracic canal separated by an echogenic septum with posterior shadowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A split cord divided by an osseous or cartilaginous septum, which casts a shadow, is diastematomyelia (split cord malformation type I), often with tethering. The normal central echo complex is a single thin bright line within one cord.
exam2.hint: Ask how many neural structures are in the canal and what separates them.

exam2.question: An infant of a mother with poorly controlled diabetes has absent lower sacral segments. Spinal ultrasound shows a cord ending abruptly at T12 in a blunt, wedge-shaped configuration. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Tethered cord from a thickened filum

exam2.explanation: Caudal regression, strongly associated with maternal diabetes, shows sacral agenesis with a high, abruptly terminating club- or wedge-shaped conus. A tethered cord is low-lying rather than high and blunt.
exam2.hint: Compare the shape and level of this conus with the normal tapered conus.

exam2.question: A 3-week-old has a centered femoral head with a Graf alpha angle of 46 degrees and a beta angle of 70 degrees. How is this hip classified?
exam2.explanation: An alpha angle of 43 to 49 degrees with a centered head and beta angle of 77 degrees or less is type IIc, a critical hip that needs treatment; with these alpha values and a beta angle over 77 degrees the hip is type D (decentering). Type IIa requires an alpha angle of 50 to 59 degrees.
exam2.hint: Place the alpha angle first, then use the beta angle to refine the type.

exam2.question: A newborn has a skin-covered soft lumbosacral mass. Ultrasound shows a low-lying cord ending in a placode that is continuous with an echogenic fatty mass extending through a posterior dysraphic defect into subcutaneous fat. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A skin-covered dysraphism in which an intraspinal lipoma joins the neural placode and subcutaneous fat is a lipomyelomeningocele, a cause of tethering. A myelomeningocele is an open defect without skin covering.
exam2.hint: Consider skin coverage and the tissue type bridging the defect.

exam2.question: During neonatal spinal sonography, which method is most reliable for determining the level of the conus medullaris?

options.text: Measure the distance from the skin dimple to the conus
Assume the conus lies at the level of the iliac crest
Identify the lumbosacral junction and count vertebral bodies cephalad, confirmed by the last rib-bearing vertebra
Use the end of the thecal sac as the L5 level

exam2.explanation: Counting from a reliable landmark such as the lumbosacral junction and cross-checking with the lowest rib-bearing T12 vertebra gives the most accurate level. Surface landmarks like the iliac crest vary and are not reliable for vertebral numbering.
exam2.hint: Use bony landmarks inside the spine rather than surface features.

exam2.question: Which position and transducer are standard for the Graf static coronal hip examination?

options.text: Supine with a 3 MHz curved transducer angled cephalad
Lateral decubitus with a linear transducer parallel to the long axis of the body
Prone with a phased-array transducer over the buttock
Sitting with a microconvex transducer over the groin

exam2.explanation: The Graf technique uses a lateral decubitus position, often in a positioning cradle, with a high-frequency linear transducer over the greater trochanter in a true coronal plane. Curved and sector transducers distort the straight iliac line and the angle measurements.
exam2.hint: Recall how the infant is held for the standard Graf image and what image geometry the angle measurements depend on.

exam2.question: A 6-week-old has a Graf alpha angle of 40 degrees. The femoral head is displaced superolaterally out of the acetabulum, and the labrum is everted. What is the best description of this hip?

options.text: Physiologically immature hip needing only observation

exam2.explanation: An alpha angle below 43 degrees with a displaced femoral head and everted labrum indicates a decentered hip (Graf type III or IV) needing treatment. Physiologic immaturity applies only to centered hips with angles of 50 to 59 degrees in young infants.
exam2.hint: Check whether the femoral head is still seated in the socket.

exam2.question: An infant with a dislocated hip is placed in a Pavlik harness. What is the main role of ultrasound during treatment?

options.text: Measure leg length to track growth
Confirm the femoral head is reduced while in the harness
Exclude septic arthritis before each adjustment

exam2.explanation: Ultrasound performed in the harness confirms that the femoral head is reduced and monitors acetabular development; failure to reduce within about 3 to 4 weeks prompts a change in treatment. Avascular necrosis is assessed later with radiographs or MRI.
exam2.hint: Consider which question ultrasound can answer while the infant is still wearing the device, without radiation.

exam2.question: A 6-year-old has a hard, slowly growing nodule on the cheek. Ultrasound shows a well-defined subcutaneous nodule with an echogenic center, posterior shadowing and a hypoechoic rim. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Pilomatricoma, a common benign hair-matrix tumor of the head and neck in children, is typically a calcified subcutaneous nodule with an echogenic shadowing center and hypoechoic rim. Infantile hemangiomas are highly vascular and arise in early infancy.
exam2.hint: Relate the calcified center to the patient age and location.

exam2.question: During a dynamic hip ultrasound, the femoral head moves posteriorly out of the acetabulum when the flexed hip is adducted with gentle posterior pressure and returns with release. What does this finding indicate?

options.text: Hip instability with subluxation or dislocation on stress

exam2.explanation: Posterior displacement with a Barlow-type stress maneuver indicates an unstable hip in the DDH spectrum. A normal hip stays seated with stress.
exam2.hint: Relate the maneuver to the clinical provocative test it reproduces.

exam2.question: A 13-year-old gymnast has a firm dorsal wrist lump. Ultrasound shows an anechoic, noncompressible, multilobulated lesion with a thin neck extending toward the scapholunate ligament and no internal flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Giant cell tumor of tendon sheath

exam2.explanation: A well-defined anechoic, avascular cyst with a neck tracking to the scapholunate joint is a dorsal wrist ganglion, the most common soft tissue mass of the hand and wrist. Giant cell tumor of tendon sheath is a solid, hypoechoic, often vascular mass along a tendon.
exam2.hint: Look for a connection to the joint.

exam2.question: A 13-year-old soccer player has painful swelling over the tibial tuberosity. Ultrasound shows a fragmented, irregular tibial tubercle ossification center, a thickened hypoechoic distal patellar tendon and fluid in the deep infrapatellar bursa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Traction apophysitis at the tibial tuberosity in an active adolescent produces fragmentation, distal patellar tendon thickening and deep infrapatellar bursitis, known as Osgood-Schlatter disease. Sinding-Larsen-Johansson involves the inferior pole of the patella at the proximal end of the tendon.
exam2.hint: Locate which end of the patellar tendon is affected.

exam2.question: A 7-year-old has 3 days of fever and focal tenderness over the distal tibia. Radiographs are normal. Ultrasound shows a hypoechoic fluid collection elevating the periosteum from the cortex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Subperiosteal fluid can be detected sonographically days before radiographic bone changes in acute osteomyelitis. Cellulitis is confined to the subcutaneous tissues without periosteal elevation.
exam2.hint: Consider which deep layer is lifted and why radiographs are still normal.

exam2.question: A 3-month-old has a rapidly growing soft red mass on the back that appeared at 2 weeks of age. Ultrasound shows a well-defined solid lesion with high vessel density and arterial and venous waveforms, without phleboliths. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Infantile hemangioma in the proliferative phase

exam2.explanation: Infantile hemangiomas appear shortly after birth, proliferate in infancy and later involute, and are solid with high vessel density. Venous malformations are compressible, low-flow and may contain phleboliths.
exam2.hint: Use the natural history, appearing after birth and growing quickly.

exam2.question: A 14-year-old has a soft bluish forearm mass that enlarges when the arm hangs down. Ultrasound shows compressible hypoechoic channels with slow monophasic venous flow and echogenic shadowing foci. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Compressible slow-flow channels that enlarge when dependent and contain phleboliths are typical of venous malformation. An arteriovenous malformation has high-flow arterialized signals without a solid matrix.
exam2.hint: Consider what the shadowing foci and the change with arm position say about flow in this lesion.

exam2.question: A newborn delivered after shoulder dystocia does not move the right arm. Ultrasound over the right clavicle shows cortical discontinuity with angulation and a surrounding hypoechoic hematoma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Clavicle fracture is the most common birth fracture, and ultrasound shows the cortical break, displacement and hematoma without radiation; it can coexist with brachial plexus injury. A normal clavicle has a continuous echogenic cortex.
exam2.hint: Trace the cortex along its full length.

exam2.question: A 7-year-old has a soft swelling behind the knee. Ultrasound shows an anechoic cyst typical of a popliteal (Baker) cyst. Between which two structures does the neck of the cyst extend?

options.text: Lateral head of the gastrocnemius and biceps femoris
Medial head of the gastrocnemius and semimembranosus tendon

exam2.explanation: A popliteal cyst arises from the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa, so its neck lies between the medial gastrocnemius head and the semimembranosus tendon. Lateral structures are not involved in this bursa.
exam2.hint: Picture the posteromedial knee bursa.

exam2.question: In the Graf method of infant hip sonography, which features must be seen to confirm the standard coronal plane?

options.text: The greater trochanter, ischial tuberosity and pubic symphysis
The femoral shaft, patella and tibial plateau
The sacroiliac joint, iliac crest and gluteal fold
A straight iliac line, the inferior tip of the ilium and the acetabular labrum

exam2.explanation: The standard plane requires a straight horizontal ilium, the lower limb of the ilium in the acetabular fossa and the labrum; otherwise angles are unreliable. Trochanter and pubic structures are not plane criteria.
exam2.hint: Think about which landmarks define the acetabular roof lines.

exam2.question: A 16-year-old with a sore throat for a week now has high fever, a tender swollen left neck and new chest radiograph nodules. Neck ultrasound shows an enlarged, noncompressible left internal jugular vein filled with echogenic material and no color flow, with surrounding inflamed soft tissue. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein (Lemierre syndrome)

exam2.explanation: Internal jugular vein thrombosis after pharyngitis, with fever and septic pulmonary emboli, is Lemierre syndrome, usually from Fusobacterium necrophorum. Jugular phlebectasia is a compressible, dilated vein with preserved flow that enlarges with Valsalva.
exam2.hint: Check whether the dilated vein compresses and contains flow, then link it to the recent throat infection and lung findings.

exam2.question: A 10-year-old has a painless submandibular swelling. Ultrasound shows a thin-walled anechoic cyst in the sublingual space that extends posteriorly around the free edge of the mylohyoid muscle into the submandibular space, with a tapering tail. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A ranula is a mucus retention cyst of the sublingual gland; the plunging type extends into the submandibular space, and a tail reaching into the sublingual space is the key sign. Thyroglossal duct cysts are midline near the hyoid.
exam2.hint: Trace the tail back to the space it came from.

exam2.question: A 14-year-old girl with weight loss, tremor and suppressed TSH has a diffusely enlarged thyroid with markedly increased vascularity throughout the gland on color Doppler. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Diffuse enlargement with intense parenchymal hypervascularity (thyroid inferno) in a hyperthyroid adolescent is typical of Graves disease. Subacute thyroiditis causes painful, patchy hypoechoic areas with reduced vascularity.
exam2.hint: Pair the thyroid function result with the Doppler pattern.

exam2.question: An 8-year-old has a fluctuant mass at the angle of the mandible that enlarged after an upper respiratory infection. Ultrasound shows a cyst anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, posterior to the submandibular gland and lateral to the carotid artery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: The classic location of a second branchial cleft cyst is anterior to the SCM, posterolateral to the submandibular gland and lateral to the carotid sheath. Thyroglossal duct cysts are midline.
exam2.hint: Use the relationship to the sternocleidomastoid and carotid.

exam2.question: A 6-year-old has a third episode of painful unilateral parotid swelling without stones. Ultrasound shows an enlarged parotid with multiple small, round hypoechoic foci scattered throughout the gland. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Juvenile recurrent parotitis shows multiple small hypoechoic foci of sialectasis within an enlarged gland and usually resolves by puberty. Infantile hemangioma presents in infancy as a solid, highly vascular mass.
exam2.hint: Weigh the recurrent course along with the diffuse pattern.

exam2.question: An infant has a persistent left lower lobe opacity on chest radiograph. Ultrasound shows a solid, echogenic, lung-like mass at the left base, and color Doppler shows a feeding artery arising directly from the descending aorta. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A systemic arterial supply from the aorta to a basal lung mass identifies bronchopulmonary sequestration, which most often involves the left lower lobe. Pneumonia is supplied by pulmonary arteries and typically shows air bronchograms.
exam2.hint: Determine where the mass gets its blood supply.

exam2.question: A 15-year-old with night sweats has painless supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Which sonographic feature of the nodes is most suspicious for malignancy such as lymphoma?

options.text: Oval shape with an echogenic fatty hilum
Round shape with loss of the echogenic fatty hilum

exam2.explanation: Malignant nodes tend to be round with loss of the fatty hilum and peripheral or chaotic vascularity. Oval nodes with an echogenic hilum and hilar flow are typical of reactive nodes.
exam2.hint: Compare node shape and internal architecture with a benign reactive pattern.

exam2.question: A term infant delivered by cesarean section has tachypnea in the first hours of life. Lung ultrasound shows dense, compact B-lines in the lower lung fields and fewer B-lines above them with a sharp boundary between the two, normal pleural sliding and no consolidation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: The double lung point, a sharp transition between dense B-lines in the lower fields and more normal upper fields, is characteristic of transient tachypnea of the newborn from retained fetal lung fluid. Pneumothorax abolishes sliding and B-lines, and pneumonia shows consolidation.
exam2.hint: Consider how fluid distribution, rather than consolidation or free air, could create a sharp boundary between lung zones.

exam2.question: To detect a small pleural effusion in a child who can sit upright, where should the transducer be placed?

options.text: Anterior chest at the second intercostal space
Posterior or posterolateral chest at the costophrenic recess
Over the sternum in the midline

exam2.explanation: Pleural fluid collects in the most dependent part of the pleural space, the posterior costophrenic recess in an upright patient, where the diaphragm and liver or spleen serve as landmarks. The anterior chest is nondependent and is where free air, not fluid, collects.
exam2.hint: Gravity decides where small amounts of fluid settle.

exam2.question: A 3-year-old has fever and cough. Lung ultrasound shows a hypoechoic tissue-like region in the right lower lobe with branching echogenic air bronchograms that move with respiration. Which diagnosis do the moving air bronchograms favor?
exam2.explanation: Dynamic air bronchograms indicate patent airways within consolidated lung, favoring pneumonia. Static bronchograms are more typical of obstructive atelectasis.
exam2.hint: Ask whether air in the bronchi can still move with breathing.

exam2.question: A 9-year-old has a tender right axillary swelling 2 weeks after being scratched on the right hand by a new kitten. Ultrasound shows several enlarged, oval, hypoechoic axillary lymph nodes with preserved hilar vascularity, surrounding echogenic edematous fat and one small central hypoechoic area. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Regional lymphadenitis draining the site of a kitten scratch, with enlarged hypoechoic nodes, hilar flow, perinodal edema and sometimes small suppurative foci, is typical of Bartonella henselae infection. Lymphoma nodes are usually painless, round and lose the fatty hilum.
exam2.hint: Match the involved nodal group to the drainage of the recent injury.

exam2.question: A 3-year-old boy has urinary retention and hematuria. Pelvic ultrasound shows a lobulated, polypoid solid mass arising from the bladder base with grape-like clusters projecting into the lumen and internal flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common bladder and prostate tumor in young children, and the botryoid subtype forms grape-like polypoid masses. Transitional cell carcinoma is rare in children.
exam2.hint: Think about which childhood tumor arises at the bladder base and grows into the lumen as polypoid masses.

exam2.question: An 8-year-old boy has a rapidly enlarging abdomen over 2 weeks. Ultrasound shows markedly thickened hypoechoic bowel walls, bulky hypoechoic mesenteric masses and ascites. Serum LDH is very high. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Rapid growth, very hypoechoic bowel wall thickening, mesenteric masses and high LDH typify Burkitt lymphoma, among the fastest-growing human tumors. Crohn disease does not grow this quickly or form bulky masses.
exam2.hint: Consider which tumor doubles in size within days.

exam2.question: A 7-year-old with leukemia has persistent fever as the neutrophil count recovers after chemotherapy. Ultrasound shows multiple small lesions in the liver and spleen, each with a hypoechoic rim, an echogenic ring and a central hypoechoic nidus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
